prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Alphabet Inc." (ticker GOOGL), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "GOOGL", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Alphabet Inc.
result.industry: Internet search, digital advertising, cloud computing and AI
markets: Cloud computing and AI infrastructure (Google Cloud)
Mobile operating systems and app stores (Android, Google Play)
Consumer subscriptions and devices (YouTube Premium, Google One, Pixel)

mission.statement: to organize the world's information and make it universally accessible and useful
mission.plain: Help everyone find and use any information they need.

about.plain: Alphabet owns Google. It runs the search box most people use to look things up, plus YouTube, Gmail, Google Maps, Chrome and the Android software inside most phones. These are free to use, and Google earns money by showing ads next to them. It also rents out powerful computers and AI, such as its Gemini helper, to businesses, and owns Waymo, which runs robot taxis with no driver.
about.customers: Mostly businesses that pay to show ads, plus companies that rent its cloud computers and people who pay for subscriptions like YouTube Premium.
about.everyday: When you 'google' something, watch a YouTube video or use Maps on an Android phone, you are using Alphabet's products.

money.plain: ads shown next to search results and in Maps
renting computers, AI chips and work apps to businesses
YouTube Premium, YouTube TV, Google One, Play Store, Pixel phones
ads it places on other websites and apps
an AI helper and AI models sold to people and companies
driverless robotaxi rides and other early projects

result.summary: Alphabet has one of the widest moats in business: Google Search holds roughly 90% of global search, fed by data from billions of users, default placement on Android, Chrome and Apple devices, and an advertiser network that no rival matches. Its own TPU chips, DeepMind research and Gemini models give it a full-stack AI position, and Google Cloud is growing fast (revenue up about 80% year on year in Q2 2026). The main risk is that AI chatbots change how people search and that antitrust remedies weaken its default deals.

pricingPower.evidence: Search ad prices are set by auctions where Google controls most of the demand, so cost-per-click has kept rising while paid clicks also grew; Search revenue still rose about 17% in Q2 2026 to $63.3B. Google raised Workspace prices in 2025 while bundling Gemini, and has raised YouTube Premium and YouTube TV prices repeatedly with subscriber numbers still growing.

moats.evidence: 'Google' is a verb in many languages and is regularly ranked among the world's most valuable brands; YouTube, Android, Chrome and Gmail are each household names with billions of users.

Gmail, Drive, Photos, Android and Workspace hold users' data and habits, and advertisers have built their campaign tools around Google Ads; switching search engines itself is easy, which limits this moat.
More searches give better results and more advertisers, which brings more users; YouTube's creator-viewer-advertiser flywheel and Android's app developer ecosystem work the same way.
Its own TPU chips and global data centres give it among the lowest costs per AI query, and it planned $175-185B of 2026 capex that few rivals can afford.
Search and video sharing have room for only one or two global players, so a new entrant would struggle to earn a return on the investment needed.
Alphabet is more often the incumbent being counter-positioned: AI answer engines such as ChatGPT and Perplexity threaten the ad-supported results page.
Over 25 years of ranking, ad-auction and data-centre engineering, plus DeepMind (AlphaFold, Gemini) and the invention of the Transformer in 2017, give it know-how that is hard to copy.
It owns huge proprietary data sets (search logs, YouTube's video library, Maps) and the default search deal with Apple, though courts limited exclusive default contracts in 2025.

customers.evidence: Google Search keeps about 90% global share despite rivals being one click away, YouTube is the most used video platform, and the Gemini app reached 950 million monthly users by mid-2026; advertisers keep coming back because Google ads have measurable returns.

talent.evidence: Google has topped employer rankings for years (Fortune's Best Companies to Work For number one many times) and remains a top destination for engineers and AI researchers, with DeepMind holding two 2024 Nobel prizes (Hassabis and Jumper); it lost some AI researchers to high-paying rivals like Meta and OpenAI.

product.evidence: Google Search, Chrome, Android, YouTube and Maps are the market leaders, and Gemini 3 models topped public leaderboards such as LMArena after launch in late 2025; Google's TPUs are one of the few credible alternatives to NVIDIA GPUs.

competitors.name: Microsoft
competitors.note: Bing search, Copilot AI assistant, Azure cloud, Microsoft 365 vs Workspace

competitors.name: OpenAI
competitors.note: ChatGPT competes with Search and Gemini for questions and AI subscriptions

competitors.name: Meta Platforms
competitors.note: digital advertising budgets, Instagram Reels vs YouTube, Llama vs Gemini

competitors.name: Amazon
competitors.note: AWS vs Google Cloud, product search ads, Prime Video vs YouTube

competitors.name: Apple
competitors.note: iOS vs Android, Safari vs Chrome, devices; also a key Search distribution partner

competitors.note: short video and ad budgets vs YouTube Shorts; Doubao AI

competitors.note: Claude models compete with Gemini for enterprise AI (Alphabet is also an investor and cloud supplier)

competitors.note: AI answer engine and browser vs Search and Chrome

competitors.name: Baidu
competitors.note: search and robotaxis (Apollo Go vs Waymo)

threats: AI chatbots and answer engines (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, Meta AI) taking search queries and ad budgets away from the classic results page
US antitrust remedies: the 2025 search ruling bans exclusive default deals and forces some data sharing, and the ad-tech case could force changes to or sale of parts of its ad exchange business
EU Digital Markets Act enforcement and fines, including the 2025 €2.95B ad-tech fine
Very heavy AI spending ($175-185B capex planned for 2026) that may not earn adequate returns and is already squeezing free cash flow
Losing default placement on Apple devices or in browsers if payments to partners are restricted
Short video competition from TikTok and Instagram Reels for viewers and advertisers

ceo.name: Sundar Pichai
ceo.background: metallurgical engineer (IIT Kharagpur), MS in materials science from Stanford, Wharton MBA; ran Chrome and Android, Google CEO since 2015 and Alphabet CEO since December 2019

c1.evidence: Alphabet is one of the leaders of generative AI, the fastest growing major industry, with Gemini at 950 million monthly app users and Google Cloud revenue up about 80% year on year to $24.8B in Q2 2026.

c2.evidence: People choose Google for the best results and habit, and advertisers for unmatched reach and measurable returns; 25 years of data, default distribution and its own TPU chips make that advantage hard to copy.

c3.evidence: Google is the textbook default leader whose name became a verb, with about 90% of global search and billions of users of YouTube, Android, Chrome and Gmail.

c4.evidence: Its mission 'to organize the world's information and make it universally accessible and useful' has guided it since 1998 and now drives its AI push, and projects like AlphaFold show purpose beyond profit, though advertising revenue still dominates decisions.

c6.evidence: “useful, smart, everywhere, dominant” — the impression is mostly positive, with people relying on its free tools, though many also associate it with privacy concerns, ads and monopoly power.

c7.evidence: It rides several secular trends at once: digital advertising, cloud computing, generative AI and autonomous driving, each a market worth hundreds of billions of dollars and growing.

c8.evidence: Its AI and computing platform lets it expand into AI agents, selling TPU chips to outside customers, robotaxis (Waymo), quantum computing (Willow chip) and drug discovery (Isomorphic Labs).

m1.evidence: Pichai declared Google 'AI-first' in 2016, years before ChatGPT, and has steered the company to a full-stack AI strategy spanning chips, models and products.

m2.evidence: Pichai is not a founder but has served the company since 2004 and invests for the long term (TPUs, Waymo, quantum), while founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin keep voting control and Brin has returned to work on Gemini.

m4.evidence: Pichai is known as a calm, consensus-building leader who listens to staff, but his tenure has included 12,000 layoffs in 2023 and firings after employee protests.

m5.evidence: Google's culture of engineering invention long predates Pichai; he merged Google Brain and DeepMind in 2023 to restore AI speed after ChatGPT exposed slow product shipping.

m6.evidence: Pichai is an engineer by training who led the Chrome and Android product teams and speaks in detail about models, chips and products.

m7.evidence: Pichai is widely seen as thoughtful and decent, and has promoted programmes like Google.org, AI for science (AlphaFold) and responsible AI principles.

m7b.evidence: Pichai gave the 2017 Carnegie Mellon University commencement address and the virtual 'Dear Class of 2020' speech on YouTube, but no Stanford, Harvard or MIT commencement that I can confirm.

m8b.evidence: Pichai is respected but low-key and diplomatic, the opposite of a flamboyant personality like Musk or Karp.

m9.evidence: Since he became Alphabet CEO in late 2019 revenue has more than doubled from $162B (2019) to $403B (2025), and Google Cloud went from heavy losses to $8.8B operating profit in Q2 2026.

m10.evidence: Google is famous for lavish perks, but since 2022 Pichai has driven efficiency drives, cut staff and benefits, and lifted operating margin from 23% in 2020 to 32% in 2025.

c10.evidence: Free Search, Maps, YouTube, Gmail, Translate and Android serve billions of people worldwide, including many in poorer countries who rely on cheap Android phones.

p2.evidence: Running planet-scale search, training frontier AI models on its own chips and building driverless cars are among the hardest engineering feats in the world.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose every year from $182.5B in 2020 to $402.8B in 2025.

f2.evidence: Gross margin rose from about 54% in 2020 to about 60% in 2025 and operating margin from about 23% to 32%.

f3.evidence: At June 2026 it held $242B of cash and marketable securities against $98B of long-term debt, with $165B of 2025 operating cash flow and positive equity.

f4.evidence: Operating income grew from $41.2B in 2020 to $129.0B in 2025 and operating cash flow from $65.1B to $164.7B.

v1.evidence: Google Search is the best at finding the right answer quickly and is free and built into almost every device, a reason ordinary people understand.

v2.evidence: Google was number one on Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For many times in the 2000s and 2010s and remains among the most sought-after employers for engineers, though its perk culture has been trimmed and recent rankings are less consistent.

c5.evidence: If Google vanished overnight billions of people would lose their main way to search, navigate, email and watch videos, and millions of small businesses would lose their main advertising channel.
